name: The Raft Consensus Algorithm
statement: Raft achieves distributed consensus on a replicated log by electing a single leader per term who unilaterally manages log replication to followers.
statementAccent: electing a single leader per term who unilaterally manages log replication
meaning: Raft, introduced by Diego Ongaro and John Ousterhout in their 2014 paper "In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm," keeps a replicated log consistent across a cluster of servers so they can implement the same replicated state machine. It was explicitly designed as an easier-to-understand alternative to Paxos while providing equivalent correctness and efficiency.
mechanism: Raft decomposes consensus into three subproblems: leader election (servers use randomised timeouts to become candidates and win a leader role via majority vote for a numbered "term"), log replication (the leader appends client commands to its log and replicates them, committing once a majority store an entry), and safety (rules ensuring a newly elected leader holds all previously committed entries). Servers act as leader, follower, or candidate, and leader heartbeats prevent unnecessary elections.

examples.text: If a follower receives no heartbeat within its randomised election timeout, it becomes a candidate, increments the term, and requests votes to become the new leader.

A leader appends a client command to its log and replicates it to followers via AppendEntries RPCs; once a majority durably store the entry, the leader considers it committed and applies it to the state machine.
Raft underlies widely used systems such as etcd (Kubernetes’ coordination store), HashiCorp Consul, CockroachDB, and Apache Kafka’s KRaft mode.

whyItMatters: Raft’s emphasis on understandability made distributed consensus far more accessible to engineers and students than Paxos had been, a user study in the original paper found students learned Raft more easily, driving its rapid, widespread adoption in production infrastructure.
limits: Raft is not Byzantine fault tolerant (it assumes servers fail by stopping, not by acting maliciously) and it relies on a single leader per term, which can create a temporary availability gap during elections and a throughput bottleneck since all writes flow through one node.
misreadings: Raft is sometimes assumed to guarantee strict linearizable reads from any replica without qualification; in practice safe linearizable reads require additional mechanisms such as leader leases or read-index checks, and its guarantees apply only under its non-Byzantine failure model.
origin: Devised by Diego Ongaro and John Ousterhout of Stanford University; the paper was presented at USENIX ATC 2014 and received a Best Paper Award.

sources.text: Raft (algorithm), Wikipedia. — the authorship, design goals, roles/terms/election mechanics, the non-Byzantine limitation, and production adopters.
Ongaro & Ousterhout, "In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm," USENIX ATC 2014. — the origin and design.
